\chapter{Sorry}
\label{ch:ka-sorry}
\hlchaptermodality{9}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can apologise in Kannada and ask someone to forgive me.}

Say \kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}, trace it back through kṣamisu to Sanskrit kṣamā, and contrast it with Tamil's unrelated maṉṉikkavum.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}]{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ} (kṣamisi) — forgive me / sorry}

\label{lesson:KA-C09-kshamisi}



\begin{quote}
You already know \textbf{\kn{ದಯವಿಟ್ಟು}}, \textquotedblleft{}please.\textquotedblright{} Kannada's \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} reuses a trick you'll see everywhere in this language: taking a Sanskrit noun and turning it into a working Kannada verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಾ}} (\emph{kṣamā}) = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{patience, forbearance, forgiveness}\textquotedblright{} — a Sanskrit noun, unchanged.
  \item \textbf{‑\kn{ಇಸು}} (\emph{‑isu}) = a \textbf{verb-making suffix}: bolt it onto a Sanskrit noun and you get a brand-new Kannada verb. \emph{kṣamā} + \emph{‑isu} $\to$ \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸು}} (\emph{kṣamisu}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to forgive}.\textquotedblright{} (The same move builds \kn{ಪ್ರಾರಂಭಿಸು} \emph{prārambhisu}, \textquotedblleft{}to begin,\textquotedblright{} from Sanskrit \emph{prārambha}.)
  \item \textbf{‑\kn{ಿ}} (\emph{‑i}) = the plain \textbf{imperative} ending — the very one you met on \emph{kuḷitukoḷḷi} (\textquotedblleft{}please sit\textquotedblright{}) in the please lesson.
\end{itemize}

So \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} is simply \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{forgive!}\textquotedblright{} — \emph{kṣamisu} wearing its imperative ending.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{cousinweb}
Three of the four Dravidian cousins build \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} from the very same Sanskrit noun, each with its own verb-making suffix and its own imperative shape:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Kannada \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{si}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑isu} (verb) + \textbf{‑i} (imperative)
  \item Telugu \textbf{\te{క్షమించండి}} \emph{kṣamin̄\textbf{caṇḍi}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣamā} + \textbf{‑in̄cu} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇḍi} (imperative)
  \item Malayalam \textbf{\ml{ക്ഷമിക്കണം}} \emph{kṣami\textbf{kkaṇaṁ}} — Sanskrit \emph{kṣama} + \textbf{‑ikkuka} (verb) + \textbf{‑aṇaṁ} (necessitative)
  \item Tamil \textbf{\ta{மன்னிக்கவும்}} \emph{maṉṉi\textbf{kkavum}} — its \textbf{own} native root \emph{maṉṉi}, not Sanskrit at all
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} is a genuine, everyday way to say \textquotedblleft{}sorry\textquotedblright{} — not overly formal — but in casual conversation you'll also hear the softer \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ} \kn{ಬಿಡಿ}} (\emph{kṣamisi biḍi}, roughly \textquotedblleft{}just forgive {[}it{]}\textquotedblright{}) or simply the borrowed English \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sorry},\textquotedblright{} which is extremely common in spoken Kannada.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kṣamā\textquotedblright{} — the Sanskrit noun, patience/forgiveness
  \item the verb — \textquotedblleft{}kṣamisu,\textquotedblright{} to forgive — then \textquotedblleft{}kṣamisi,\textquotedblright{} forgive!
  \item contrast — Tamil's maṉṉikkavum uses its own root instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \textbf{\kn{ಕ್ಷಮಿಸಿ}} built from? (\textbf{Sanskrit kṣamā} \textquotedblleft{}forgiveness\textquotedblright{} + the verb-making suffix \textbf{‑isu} + the imperative \textbf{‑i}.) Which cousin languages do the same trick, and which one doesn't? (\textbf{Telugu and Malayalam} also verb-ify \emph{kṣamā}; \textbf{Tamil} uses its own native root \emph{maṉṉi} instead.) What do people often say casually instead? (\textbf{Kṣamisi biḍi}, or simply borrowed English \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{sorry}.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\kn{◌ಿ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S04-vowel-sign-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{◌್} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ಿ}} — \emph{i}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{i}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{◌ಿ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸರಿ}} \emph{sari} — okay / alright / correct (sari)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā} — how are you? (respectful)
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ}} \emph{cennāgi} — well, nicely — and the reply "\kn{ನಾನು} \kn{ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿದ್ದೇನೆ}
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಪರವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ}} \emph{paravāgilla} — it's okay / no problem / you're welcome
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ಿ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ಿ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌ಿ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ಸರಿ}  ·  \kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?  ·  \kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌ಿ} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{◌ಿ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{◌ಿ}? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (\textbf{Puts \emph{i} on; takes the built-in \emph{a} off.}) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ḷa]{\kn{ಳ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:KA-S113-letter-lla}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಗ} — what does it do?

One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಳ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಳ}} — \emph{ḷa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ḷ}, it is \textbf{ḷa}.

You already say these, and every one of them has \kn{ಳ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನಾಳೆ} \kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} \emph{nāḷe sigōṇa} — see you tomorrow
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಆರು} \kn{ಏಳು} \kn{ಎಂಟು} \kn{ಒಂಬತ್ತು} \kn{ಹತ್ತು}} — six to ten
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಳ} — copy what you see}
Put your pen on \kn{ಳ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{ಳ} in the ones that have it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಳ} three times, saying \emph{ḷa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \kn{ಳ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \kn{ಳ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{ḷa}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
